lesson.subtitle: Lesson 15 -- Food, Culture & Daily Life
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Felipe Pimenta | Lesson 15 -- Food, Culture & Daily Life

listenings.text: I move senior people between countries for a living, and the part everybody prepares for is the interview. The part that actually decides it is the dinner afterwards. Nobody tells you that, so let me. By the time they take you out, they have already decided you can do the job. What they are testing over dinner is whether they want to sit next to you for the next five years. And that is not tested with your best English. It is tested with your easiest English. Small talk is not small. It is the ten minutes in which a stranger decides whether you are down-to-earth or hard work. So when someone asks what you do outside the office, do not give them your CV again. Give them the one thing you are genuinely into, whatever it happens to be, and then hand the conversation back. That is the move most people miss. They answer, and then they stop, and the table goes quiet. Ask something back. And if you truly do not know what to say, ask about food. Everybody eats, everybody has an opinion, and nobody in the world can resist telling you where the best place in their city is.

I have cooked in four countries, and I get asked the same question in every one of them: where is the best restaurant in town. It is the wrong question, and I never answer it. A hidden gem almost never looks like a gem from the street. It has a bad sign, six tables, one thing on the menu, and a queue of people who all seem to know each other. The famous place on the square, the one with the beautiful photographs, is usually overrated, and everybody knows it, and everybody books it anyway. So here is what to ask instead. Do not ask a stranger where the best restaurant is. Ask them where they ate with their family last Sunday. You will get a completely different answer, and a much better dinner. And one more thing, about being far from home. When people say they are homesick, they think they miss the country. They do not. They miss one specific plate of food, cooked badly, in a kitchen that was too small. That is what comfort food really is. Learn to make yours before you move, and the first month abroad is a different month entirely.

items.situation: Someone at the table asks: "So what do you do outside work?"
tips: I'm really into cooking, actually -- I did a French course and an Italian one. Do you cook at all?
Answer, add the thing you are into, then hand it back. Never stop on your own answer.

items.situation: You want to check something you half-know: this person is not from the city.
tips: You're not from here originally, are you?
Negative sentence takes a positive tag. It is a check, not an interrogation.

items.situation: Someone says: "I don't eat much meat."
tips: Neither do I, most of the week.
Agreeing with a negative takes Neither, never too.

items.situation: Someone says: "I lived in Liverpool for a year."
tips: Did you? What was that like?
Echo the auxiliary and hand the turn straight back. That is how a rally continues.

items.situation: You want to invite a colleague out on Friday.
tips: Are you up for grabbing a bite on Friday? I know a hidden gem.
Up for plus -ing is the natural, low-register invitation.

items.situation: The bill arrives and your colleague reaches for it.
tips: Put that away -- this one is on me. You can get the next one.
Short, warm, and it quietly books a next time.
